decks.title: Alkanes — Part 1: Classification, isomerism, conformations and preparation
goals: Classify hydrocarbons and name alkanes by IUPAC rules, including the isomers of pentane
Draw staggered and eclipsed ethane in Sawhorse and Newman projections and explain their stability
Write equations for preparing alkanes by decarboxylation, Kolbe electrolysis, Wurtz reaction, Corey–House synthesis and from aldehydes and Grignard reagents

slides.heading: Hydrocarbons and the place of alkanes
slides.body_md: **Hydrocarbons** contain only carbon and hydrogen. They are **open-chain (aliphatic)** or **closed-chain (cyclic)**; the open-chain ones are **saturated** (alkanes, only C–C single bonds) or **unsaturated** (alkenes and alkynes). Cyclic ones are **alicyclic** (cycloalkanes) or **aromatic** (benzene and its derivatives).

visual.alt: Flow chart classifying hydrocarbons into open chain saturated and unsaturated, and closed chain alicyclic and aromatic

slides.narration: Welcome to the study of alkanes. Hydrocarbons are compounds of carbon and hydrogen only. They are classified by their carbon skeleton. Open chain compounds are either saturated, the alkanes, or unsaturated, the alkenes and alkynes. Closed chain compounds are alicyclic, such as cyclohexane, or aromatic, such as benzene. In this part we look at alkanes, their structures, shapes and preparation.

slides.heading: Homologous series and the general formula
slides.body_md: Alkanes form a **homologous series** with general formula **CₙH₂ₙ₊₂**: each member differs from the next by **–CH₂–** (14 mass units) and they show a gradual change in properties. Every carbon is **sp³** hybridised, with tetrahedral bond angles of about 109.5° and C–C bonds of 154 pm.

visual.alt: Table of the first ten unbranched alkanes with name, molecular formula, boiling point in degrees Celsius and physical state at 298 kelvin

slides.narration: The alkanes form a homologous series. Each member differs from the next by one carbon and two hydrogens, a methylene group, and the general formula is C n H two n plus two. Every carbon atom is sp three hybridised, so the bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron at about one hundred and nine and a half degrees. The first four members are gases and the next are liquids.

slides.heading: Naming alkanes by IUPAC rules
slides.body_md: (1) Choose the **longest continuous carbon chain** as the parent. (2) Number it from the end that gives the **lowest locant** to the first branch (or the lowest set of locants). (3) Name branches as alkyl groups; list them in **alphabetical order**. (4) Use di-, tri- for repeated groups (ignored in alphabetising). (5) Write: locants–substituents then parent.

visual.alt: Flow chart of the steps in naming an alkane: longest chain, lowest locants, alphabetical order, then writing the name

slides.narration: To name an alkane, follow four steps. First find the longest continuous chain; that gives the parent name. Next number the chain from the end that gives the lowest numbers to the branches. Then name each branch as an alkyl group and arrange them in alphabetical order. Finally write the locants, the substituent names and the parent name together, using di or tri when a group repeats.

slides.heading: Chain isomerism: the isomers of pentane
slides.body_md: Alkanes show **chain isomerism**. Butane has 2 isomers, **pentane has 3**, hexane 5, heptane 9 and octane 18. The three isomers of C₅H₁₂ are **pentane**, **2-methylbutane** (isopentane) and **2,2-dimethylpropane** (neopentane); they differ in physical properties such as boiling point.

slides.narration: Alkanes with four or more carbon atoms show chain isomerism. Pentane has three isomers. Pentane itself has a straight chain. Two methylbutane has one methyl branch on the second carbon. Two two dimethylpropane has two methyl groups on the same carbon and is the most compact. They have the same molecular formula but different boiling points.

slides.heading: Worked example: naming a branched alkane
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Name $\ce{(CH3)3C-CH2-CH(CH3)2}$.

**Solution.** The longest chain has **5 carbons** (pentane). Numbering from the left puts branches at 2, 2, 4; from the right at 2, 4, 4. The first set is lower. Three methyl groups: **2,2,4-trimethylpentane** (isooctane, C₈H₁₈, the reference fuel for octane number).

visual.alt: Table with the steps in naming 2,2,4-trimethylpentane: parent chain, branches, locants and name

slides.narration: Let us name this compound. The longest chain has five carbons, so the parent is pentane. There are three methyl branches. Numbering from the left gives the locants two, two, four, while numbering from the right gives two, four, four. The first set is lower, so we choose it. The name is two two four trimethylpentane, also called isooctane, the standard fuel for octane rating.

slides.heading: Occurrence of alkanes
slides.body_md: **Natural gas** is mainly methane (with some ethane, propane and butane); **biogas** and marsh gas are also mostly methane, formed by anaerobic decay. **Petroleum** is a complex mixture of alkanes (with cycloalkanes and aromatics) that is separated by fractional distillation into fractions of rising boiling range.

visual.alt: Table of petroleum fractions with carbon range and uses

slides.narration: Alkanes occur in nature mainly as natural gas and petroleum. Natural gas and biogas are largely methane. Petroleum is a complex mixture separated by fractional distillation. The lightest fraction is refinery gas and bottled gas, then petrol, kerosene and diesel, and finally lubricating oil, wax and bitumen. The heavier the fraction, the more carbon atoms in its molecules.

slides.heading: Conformations: Sawhorse and Newman projections
slides.body_md: **Conformations** are the different arrangements of atoms produced by rotation about a **single bond**. In ethane the extremes are **staggered** (C–H bonds 60° apart) and **eclipsed** (0° apart). A **Sawhorse** projection views the C–C bond obliquely; a **Newman** projection looks along it, the front carbon at the centre and the rear carbon as the circle. **Methane** has no C–C bond, so it has only one arrangement.

slides.narration: Rotation about the carbon carbon single bond of ethane gives different arrangements called conformations. The two extremes are the staggered form and the eclipsed form. In a sawhorse projection we look at the bond from an angle. In a Newman projection we look straight down the bond; the front carbon is the centre of the picture and the rear carbon is the circle. Methane has no carbon carbon bond, so it has no such conformations.

slides.heading: Why the staggered conformation is more stable
slides.body_md: In the **eclipsed** form the C–H bonding pairs on the two carbons are as close as possible, so repulsion (**torsional strain**) is greatest; in the **staggered** form they are farthest apart. The staggered form is lower in energy by about **12.5 kJ mol⁻¹**, the **torsional barrier**. This is small, so at room temperature ethane rotates almost freely and the conformations cannot be separated.

slides.heading: Preparation of alkanes: the main routes
slides.body_md: Alkanes are made by **decarboxylation** (loses a carbon), **Kolbe electrolysis** (joins two R groups), the **Wurtz reaction** (joins two R groups), **Corey–House synthesis** (joins two different groups), **reduction of aldehydes** and by **hydrolysis of Grignard reagents**.

rows: R–H, one carbon less than the acid

visual.alt: Table of six preparations of alkanes with starting material, reagent and carbon count

slides.narration: Here are the main ways of making alkanes. Decarboxylation of a sodium carboxylate with soda lime loses one carbon. Kolbe electrolysis and the Wurtz reaction join two alkyl groups, doubling the carbon count. Corey House synthesis joins two different groups. An aldehyde can be reduced to an alkane with zinc amalgam and hydrochloric acid, and a Grignard reagent gives an alkane with water.

slides.heading: Kolbe's electrolysis
slides.body_md: Electrolysis of **aqueous sodium or potassium carboxylate** gives an alkane at the **anode**: $2\text{RCOO}^- \rightarrow \text{R–R} + 2\text{CO}_2 + 2e^-$; hydrogen and alkali form at the cathode. Sodium ethanoate gives **ethane**; sodium propanoate gives **butane**. The method gives an alkane with an **even** number of carbon atoms (R–R) from a single salt.

slides.narration: In Kolbe electrolysis an aqueous solution of a sodium carboxylate is electrolysed between platinum electrodes. At the anode two carboxylate ions lose electrons and form an alkane with carbon dioxide. At the cathode water is reduced to hydrogen and hydroxide ions. Sodium ethanoate gives ethane. Two alkyl groups join, so the alkane has twice the carbons of the alkyl group.

slides.heading: Wurtz reaction and Corey–House synthesis
slides.body_md: **Wurtz:** an alkyl halide with sodium in dry ether gives a symmetrical alkane. With two different halides a **mixture of three alkanes** forms, so it is not suitable for odd-carbon or unsymmetrical alkanes. **Corey–House:** lithium dialkylcuprate with an alkyl halide gives a clean, unsymmetrical alkane.

visual.alt: Wurtz reaction: two bromoethane plus two sodium in dry ether gives butane and two sodium bromide
visual.caption: Wurtz: R–X to R–R

slides.narration: In the Wurtz reaction, an alkyl halide is treated with sodium metal in dry ether and two alkyl groups join. Bromoethane gives butane. With two different halides the products are a mixture of three alkanes that are hard to separate, so the method suits symmetrical alkanes only. The Corey House synthesis uses a lithium dialkylcuprate with an alkyl halide to join two different groups cleanly.

slides.heading: Worked example: choosing the Wurtz halide
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Which alkyl halide gives **2,5-dimethylhexane** by the Wurtz reaction?

**Solution.** The Wurtz reaction joins two identical R groups, so cut the chain in the middle (C-3–C-4): each half is **(CH₃)₂CH–CH₂–**, 2-methylpropyl. The halide is **1-bromo-2-methylpropane**: $\ce{2(CH3)2CHCH2Br + 2Na -> (CH3)2CHCH2CH2CH(CH3)2 + 2NaBr}$.

visual.alt: Two 1-bromo-2-methylpropane plus two sodium gives 2,5-dimethylhexane and two sodium bromide

slides.narration: To make two five dimethylhexane by the Wurtz reaction, split the chain at its centre. Each half is a two methylpropyl group, so the halide is one bromo two methylpropane. Two molecules of this halide react with two atoms of sodium to give the eight carbon alkane and two formula units of sodium bromide. The carbon count is twice that of the alkyl group.

slides.heading: From aldehydes and Grignard reagents; decarboxylation
slides.body_md: **Decarboxylation:** heating sodium ethanoate with soda lime gives methane (one carbon fewer than the acid). **Aldehydes** are reduced to alkanes with zinc amalgam and conc. HCl (Clemmensen): same carbon number. **Grignard reagents** react with water (or any compound with an acidic hydrogen): $\ce{CH3MgBr + H2O -> CH4 + Mg(OH)Br}$.

visual.alt: Ethylmagnesium bromide plus water gives ethane and magnesium hydroxide bromide
visual.caption: Grignard reagent + water gives an alkane

slides.narration: Three more preparations. Heating sodium ethanoate with soda lime removes carbon dioxide as sodium carbonate and gives methane, one carbon fewer than the acid. An aldehyde is reduced to the alkane with the same number of carbons by zinc amalgam and concentrated hydrochloric acid. A Grignard reagent is converted to an alkane by water; ethylmagnesium bromide gives ethane.

Alkanes are made by decarboxylation, Kolbe electrolysis, the Wurtz reaction, Corey House synthesis, reduction of aldehydes and hydrolysis of Grignard reagents.

slides.heading: Physical properties of alkanes
slides.body_md: Alkane molecules are **non-polar**, held together only by weak **London (dispersion) forces**. These forces grow with molecular size and surface contact, which governs boiling point, melting point and density; non-polar solvents dissolve alkanes but water does not.

rows: C₁–C₄ gases; C₅–C₁₇ liquids; higher solids
Rises with chain length; falls with branching
Rises slowly but stays below 1 g mL⁻¹
Insoluble in water; soluble in non-polar solvents

visual.alt: Table of the physical properties of alkanes and their trends

slides.narration: Alkanes are non polar molecules. Only weak London dispersion forces act between them, and these forces increase with the size of the molecule. So the first four alkanes are gases, the middle ones are liquids and the higher ones are waxy solids. Alkanes do not dissolve in water but dissolve readily in non polar solvents, and they are less dense than water.

slides.heading: Boiling point and chain length
slides.body_md: Each extra –CH₂– increases the surface area and the dispersion forces, so the boiling point rises: **−161.5 °C** for methane, **36.1 °C** for pentane, **174.1 °C** for decane. The increments shrink (about 73 °C from CH₄ to C₂H₆, about 23 °C from C₉ to C₁₀).

slides.narration: The boiling point of unbranched alkanes rises steadily with the number of carbon atoms. A longer molecule has a larger surface and stronger dispersion forces, so more energy is needed to separate the molecules. Methane boils at minus one hundred sixty one degrees Celsius and decane at one hundred seventy four. The rise per added carbon becomes smaller as the chain grows longer.

slides.heading: Branching lowers the boiling point
slides.body_md: For isomers of the same molar mass, **branching** makes the molecule more **spherical** and reduces the surface area of contact, so the dispersion forces are weaker and the boiling point is lower: pentane 309 K > 2-methylbutane 301 K > 2,2-dimethylpropane 283 K. (The compact, symmetrical isomer has the higher melting point.)

slides.narration: Isomers of the same formula show how shape affects boiling point. The straight chain pentane has the largest surface area and boils at three hundred and nine kelvin. The more branched isomers are more compact, touch their neighbours over a smaller area and have weaker forces, so they boil lower. Two two dimethylpropane boils at only two hundred and eighty three kelvin.

slides.heading: Solubility and density
slides.body_md: Water molecules are strongly hydrogen bonded; alkane molecules cannot form hydrogen bonds or dipole interactions with water, so alkanes are **insoluble** in water ("like dissolves like"). They dissolve in benzene, ether and tetrachloromethane. Liquid alkanes **float** on water (density about 0.63 g mL⁻¹ for pentane to 0.73 for decane).

visual.alt: Table of densities of liquid alkanes, all below that of water

slides.narration: Alkanes cannot form hydrogen bonds or dipole interactions with water, so they do not dissolve in it. They dissolve in non polar solvents such as benzene and ether, following the rule that like dissolves like. The liquid alkanes are less dense than water, with densities between about point six three and point seven three, so they float on water.

slides.heading: Combustion
slides.body_md: Alkanes burn in excess air or oxygen to give **carbon dioxide and water** with the release of much heat; this is why they are fuels. In limited air, carbon monoxide and soot form. General equation: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ + (3n + 1)/2 O₂ → n CO₂ + (n + 1) H₂O.

visual.alt: Complete combustion of butane: two butane plus thirteen oxygen gives eight carbon dioxide and ten water
visual.caption: Complete combustion of butane

slides.narration: All alkanes burn in plenty of air to form carbon dioxide and water, and release a great deal of heat. That is why methane, propane and butane are used as fuels. For an alkane with n carbons, the oxygen needed is three n plus one over two molecules, and the products are n carbon dioxide and n plus one water. In a limited supply of air, carbon monoxide or soot forms.

slides.heading: Worked example: combustion of butane
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Butane (11.6 g, M = 58 g mol⁻¹) burns completely: $\ce{2C4H10 + 13O2 -> 8CO2 + 10H2O}$. Find the volume of O₂ at STP and the masses of CO₂ and H₂O.

**Solution.** n(C₄H₁₀) = 11.6 ÷ 58 = 0.200 mol. O₂ = 13/2 × 0.200 = 1.30 mol = 29.1 L. CO₂ = 4 × 0.200 = 0.800 mol = 35.2 g. H₂O = 5 × 0.200 = 1.00 mol = 18.0 g.

visual.alt: Table of moles and results for the complete combustion of butane

slides.narration: Work in moles. The molar mass of butane is fifty eight, so eleven point six grams is point two zero zero mole. From the equation, two moles of butane need thirteen moles of oxygen, so point two zero zero mole needs one point three zero moles, about twenty nine litres at standard conditions. It gives point eight moles of carbon dioxide, which is thirty five point two grams, and eighteen grams of water.

slides.heading: Halogenation: substitution by a free-radical chain
slides.body_md: In **diffused sunlight, ultraviolet light or at 520–670 K**, chlorine or bromine replaces H atoms of an alkane: CH₄ gives CH₃Cl, CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄. **Reactivity of halogens:** F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂ (fluorine is explosive; iodine is reversible and needs an oxidising agent). **Reactivity of C–H:** **tertiary > secondary > primary** (more stable radical).

visual.alt: Table of relative rates of abstraction of primary, secondary and tertiary hydrogen atoms by a chlorine radical

slides.narration: In ultraviolet light or at high temperature, alkanes react with chlorine or bromine by replacing hydrogen atoms, one after another. Fluorine is too violent and iodine does not react well. Among the hydrogen atoms in an alkane, tertiary ones are replaced most readily, then secondary, then primary, because the radical formed is more stable. The relative rates for chlorine are about one, three point eight and five.

slides.heading: Mechanism of the chlorination of methane
slides.body_md: A **free-radical chain** with three stages. **Initiation:** light splits Cl–Cl homolytically into 2 Cl•. **Propagation:** Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + •CH₃, then •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•; the chain repeats. **Termination:** two radicals combine and the chain ends (Cl• + Cl•, •CH₃ + Cl•, •CH₃ + •CH₃ giving ethane as a by-product).

slides.narration: The mechanism has three stages. In initiation, ultraviolet light splits a chlorine molecule into two chlorine atoms, each with an unpaired electron. In termination, two radicals combine and the chain stops.

slides.heading: Worked example: monochlorination of propane
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Propane is chlorinated in light. Using relative rates 1° : 2° = 1.0 : 3.8 (given), find the percentage of 2-chloropropane.

**Solution.** Propane has **6 primary** and **2 secondary** hydrogens. Weights: 6 × 1.0 = 6.0; 2 × 3.8 = 7.6; total 13.6. **2-Chloropropane = 7.6 ÷ 13.6 × 100 = 55.9%**; 1-chloropropane = 44.1%.

visual.alt: Table of the expected percentages of 1-chloropropane and 2-chloropropane from the chlorination of propane

slides.narration: Count the hydrogens of each kind. Propane has six primary hydrogens and two secondary ones. Multiply each number by its relative rate: six times one gives six, and two times three point eight gives seven point six. The total is thirteen point six. The share of two chloropropane is seven point six over thirteen point six, about fifty five point nine percent, and the rest is one chloropropane.

slides.heading: Catalytic oxidation
slides.body_md: With **limited oxygen and a catalyst**, alkanes are oxidised to useful compounds instead of burning completely. Methane gives **methanol** (Cu tube, 523 K, 100 atm) or **methanal** (Mo₂O₃); **ethane** is oxidised to **ethanoic acid** (manganese(II) ethanoate as catalyst).

visual.alt: Table of catalytic oxidations of methane and ethane with conditions and products

slides.narration: If an alkane is heated with a limited supply of oxygen in the presence of a catalyst, it is oxidised partially rather than burnt. Methane with copper at five hundred twenty three kelvin and one hundred atmospheres gives methanol. With molybdenum oxide it gives methanal. Ethane can be oxidised to ethanoic acid using a manganese ethanoate catalyst. These are important industrial routes.

slides.heading: Cyclisation and aromatisation
slides.body_md: Alkanes with **six or more carbons** heated at **773 K, 10–20 atm** over $\ce{Cr2O3/Al2O3}$ (or V₂O₅, Mo₂O₃) lose hydrogen and form a ring: **cyclisation** gives cyclohexane, then **aromatisation** gives benzene. Hexane → benzene + 4H₂; heptane → methylbenzene + 4H₂.

slides.narration: When hexane or higher alkanes are passed over a mixed oxide catalyst at seven hundred seventy three kelvin and high pressure, they close into rings and lose hydrogen. This ring closure is cyclisation, and the further loss of hydrogen to form a benzene ring is aromatisation. Hexane gives benzene, and heptane gives methylbenzene, with four molecules of hydrogen released in each case.

slides.heading: Isomerisation and pyrolysis
slides.body_md: **Isomerisation:** n-alkanes are converted to branched isomers by anhydrous AlCl₃ and HCl at about 573 K and 35 atm; butane gives 2-methylpropane. **Pyrolysis (cracking):** at high temperature, large alkanes break into smaller alkanes and alkenes: $\ce{C12H26 -> C7H16 + C5H10}$, and $\ce{CH4 -> C + 2H2}$ at very high temperature.

visual.alt: Isomerisation of butane to 2-methylpropane with aluminium chloride and hydrogen chloride
visual.caption: n-Butane to 2-methylpropane

slides.narration: Two more reactions. In isomerisation, a straight chain alkane is converted to a branched isomer by anhydrous aluminium chloride and hydrogen chloride; butane gives two methylpropane. In pyrolysis, also called cracking, a large alkane is heated strongly in the absence of air and breaks into smaller alkanes and alkenes. Dodecane can give heptane and pentene. Cracking supplies petrol from heavier fractions.

slides.heading: Uses of alkanes
slides.body_md: Alkanes are mainly **fuels** and **raw materials**: methane (natural gas, CNG, hydrogen, carbon black), LPG (propane + butane), petrol, kerosene and diesel, lubricating oils, paraffin wax and bitumen, and feedstock for chloroalkanes, alcohols and ethene.

rows: CNG, domestic gas; makes hydrogen and carbon black

visual.alt: Table of uses of alkanes and petroleum fractions

slides.narration: Alkanes are our main fuels. Methane is compressed natural gas and domestic gas. Propane and butane are bottled as liquefied petroleum gas. Petrol, kerosene and diesel power vehicles and aircraft. Heavier alkanes give lubricating oils, wax for candles and bitumen for roads. Alkanes are also raw materials for making hydrogen, carbon black, solvents and many other organic compounds.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Boiling point rises with chain length (dispersion forces) and falls with branching; alkanes are insoluble in water.
Combustion gives CO₂ and H₂O; catalytic oxidation gives methanol, methanal or ethanoic acid.
Halogenation is a free-radical chain: initiation, propagation, termination; reactivity 3° > 2° > 1°.
Heating over Cr₂O₃/Al₂O₃ cyclises and aromatises hexane to benzene; AlCl₃/HCl isomerises; pyrolysis cracks.

visual.alt: Summary table of reactions of alkanes and their conditions

slides.narration: To sum up Part two. The boiling point of alkanes rises with chain length and falls with branching, and alkanes do not dissolve in water. They burn to carbon dioxide and water, can be oxidised to methanol or ethanoic acid with catalysts, and react with halogens by a free radical chain. Hexane is aromatised to benzene, butane is isomerised, and large alkanes are cracked.

sections.heading: 1. Hydrocarbons, alkanes and their naming
sections.body_md: **Hydrocarbons** contain carbon and hydrogen only. **Open-chain (aliphatic)** hydrocarbons are saturated (**alkanes**) or unsaturated (alkenes, alkynes); **closed-chain (cyclic)** ones are alicyclic (cyclohexane) or aromatic (benzene). **Alkanes** have the general formula **CₙH₂ₙ₊₂**, only C–C and C–H σ bonds, sp³ carbon (bond angle about 109.5°, C–C 154 pm), and form a **homologous series** whose members differ by –CH₂– (14 u). **IUPAC naming:** longest continuous chain; lowest locants; alkyl groups in alphabetical order; di-, tri- for repeats. Example: (CH₃)₃CCH₂CH(CH₃)₂ is 2,2,4-trimethylpentane.

key_terms.definition_md: A family of compounds with the same functional group and general formula in which successive members differ by a –CH₂– unit.
A cyclic compound that is not aromatic, such as cyclohexane.

sections.heading: 2. Chain isomerism and occurrence
sections.body_md: Alkanes show **chain isomerism**. The numbers of isomers (including the straight-chain compound) for C₄ to C₈ are **2, 3, 5, 9 and 18**. **C₅H₁₂:** pentane, 2-methylbutane (isopentane) and 2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentane). **Occurrence:** natural gas and biogas (mainly **methane**, with some ethane, propane and butane) and **petroleum**, which is separated by fractional distillation into LPG, petrol, kerosene, diesel, lubricating oil, wax and bitumen.

sections.heading: 3. Conformations of ethane: Sawhorse and Newman projections
sections.body_md: **Conformations** are different arrangements of atoms obtained by rotation about a single bond. Ethane has two extremes: **staggered** (dihedral angle 60°; lowest energy) and **eclipsed** (0°; highest energy). A **Sawhorse** projection views the C–C bond obliquely; in a **Newman** projection we look along the bond: the front carbon is the centre, the rear carbon the circle. The eclipsed form is higher in energy by about **12.5 kJ mol⁻¹** (the **torsional barrier**) because the C–H bonding pairs on adjacent carbons repel most (**torsional strain**). The barrier is small, so rotation is nearly free at room temperature and the conformations cannot be isolated. **Methane** has no C–C bond and therefore only one arrangement. Energy curve: minima at 60°, 180° and 300°; maxima at 0°, 120° and 240°.

key_terms.definition_md: A spatial arrangement of atoms in a molecule produced by rotation about a single bond.
The repulsion between bonding pairs on adjacent atoms that are eclipsed.
The angle between a bond on the front carbon and a bond on the rear carbon, seen along the C–C bond.

sections.heading: 4. Preparation of alkanes
sections.body_md: **Decarboxylation:** $\ce{RCOONa + NaOH ->[CaO][\Delta] R-H + Na2CO3}$, one carbon fewer (CH₃COONa gives methane). **Kolbe electrolysis** of aqueous RCOONa: anode $2\text{RCOO}^- \rightarrow \text{R–R} + 2\text{CO}_2 + 2e^-$; cathode gives H₂ and OH⁻; sodium ethanoate gives ethane. **Wurtz:** 2RX + 2Na (dry ether) → R–R + 2NaX; a mixture of two halides gives **three alkanes**, so it is unsuitable for unsymmetrical (odd-carbon) alkanes. **Corey–House:** R₂CuLi + R′X → R–R′ (clean, unsymmetrical). **Aldehydes:** Zn–Hg/conc. HCl reduces R–CHO to R–CH₃. **Grignard reagents:** RMgX + H₂O → R–H + Mg(OH)X.

Coupling of two alkyl groups from alkyl halides with sodium in dry ether.

sections.heading: 5. Physical properties and their trends
sections.body_md: Alkanes are **non-polar**, held by weak **London dispersion forces**. **State:** C₁–C₄ gases, C₅–C₁₇ liquids, higher members solids. **Boiling point** rises with chain length (more surface, stronger forces; the rise per –CH₂– shrinks from about 73 °C to about 23 °C) and **falls with branching** (compact molecule, smaller surface): pentane 309 K > 2-methylbutane 301 K > 2,2-dimethylpropane 283 K. **Density** is below 1 g mL⁻¹ (liquid alkanes float on water). **Solubility:** insoluble in water; soluble in non-polar solvents.

key_terms.definition_md: Weak attractions between temporary dipoles in non-polar molecules, increasing with molecular surface.

sections.heading: 6. Combustion and free-radical halogenation
sections.body_md: **Combustion:** CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ + (3n + 1)/2 O₂ → n CO₂ + (n + 1) H₂O, strongly exothermic; in limited air, CO and soot form. **Halogenation** (light, or 520–670 K): a **free-radical chain** substitution. **Initiation:** Cl–Cl → 2Cl• (homolytic). **Propagation:** CH₄ + Cl• → •CH₃ + HCl; •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•. **Termination:** Cl• + Cl•, •CH₃ + Cl•, •CH₃ + •CH₃. Further substitution gives CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄ (excess methane favours CH₃Cl). **Reactivity of halogens:** F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂; **of hydrogens:** 3° > 2° > 1° (chlorination rates about 5.0 : 3.8 : 1.0). **Product ratio** = (number of H × relative rate).

key_terms.definition_md: An atom or group with an unpaired electron, written with a dot, formed by homolytic fission.
A reaction in which a reactive species is regenerated, so the steps repeat.

sections.heading: 7. Other reactions and uses
sections.body_md: **Catalytic oxidation:** 2CH₄ + O₂ → 2CH₃OH (Cu, 523 K, 100 atm); CH₄ + O₂ → HCHO + H₂O (Mo₂O₃); 2C₂H₆ + 3O₂ → 2CH₃COOH + 2H₂O (manganese ethanoate). **Cyclisation and aromatisation:** hexane → cyclohexane + H₂ → benzene + 3H₂ over Cr₂O₃/Al₂O₃ at 773 K and 10–20 atm; heptane → methylbenzene + 4H₂. **Isomerisation:** n-butane → 2-methylpropane (anhydrous AlCl₃/HCl, 573 K). **Pyrolysis (cracking):** large alkanes → smaller alkanes + alkenes (C₁₆H₃₄ → C₈H₁₈ + C₈H₁₆); CH₄ → C + 2H₂. **Uses:** fuels (CNG, LPG, petrol, kerosene, diesel), lubricants, wax, bitumen and chemical feedstock.

key_terms.definition_md: Conversion of an alkane into an aromatic hydrocarbon with loss of hydrogen.
Breaking of large molecules into smaller ones by strong heating, usually in the absence of air.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Choosing a chain that is not the longest when naming; forgetting that alphabetical order beats numerical order of the prefixes.
- Calling the eclipsed conformation more stable, or writing the dihedral angles the wrong way round (staggered 60°, eclipsed 0°).
- Writing that Kolbe electrolysis gives an alkane with one carbon fewer than the acid (that is decarboxylation).
- Saying that branching raises the boiling point.
- Drawing chlorination as an ionic reaction or leaving out the termination step.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Preparation questions: balanced equation with reagent and conditions (1 mark each), plus the name of the product.
- Mechanisms: one mark per stage (initiation, propagation, termination), with the radicals shown.
- Reasoning questions (boiling point, stability): state the trend, then give the reason in terms of surface area and dispersion forces or of torsional strain.
- Calculations: balanced equation, moles, answer with the right unit.

cards.front_md: General formula of alkanes?
cards.back_md: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.

cards.front_md: Hybridisation of carbon in alkanes and the bond angle?
cards.back_md: sp³; about 109.5°.

cards.front_md: What is a homologous series?
cards.back_md: A family with the same functional group and general formula; members differ by –CH₂– (14 u).

cards.front_md: Classify hydrocarbons.
cards.back_md: Open-chain (saturated or unsaturated) and closed-chain (alicyclic or aromatic).

cards.front_md: Rules for naming an alkane?
cards.back_md: Longest chain; lowest locants; alphabetical order of branches; di-, tri- for repeats.

cards.front_md: Number of chain isomers of C₄, C₅, C₆, C₇, C₈ alkanes?
Chain isomers of pentane?
cards.back_md: Pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane.

cards.front_md: Main constituent of natural gas and biogas?
cards.back_md: Methane.

cards.front_md: What is a conformation?
cards.back_md: An arrangement of atoms obtained by rotation about a single bond.

cards.front_md: Two extreme conformations of ethane?
cards.back_md: Staggered (60°, most stable) and eclipsed (0°, least stable).

cards.front_md: Torsional barrier of ethane?
cards.back_md: About 12.5 kJ mol⁻¹.

cards.front_md: Why is the staggered form more stable?
cards.back_md: Bonding pairs on adjacent carbons are farthest apart, so torsional strain is least.

cards.front_md: What does a Newman projection show?
cards.back_md: View along the C–C bond: front carbon at the centre, rear carbon as the circle.

cards.front_md: Why does methane have no conformations?
cards.back_md: It has no C–C bond to rotate about.

cards.front_md: Decarboxylation of sodium ethanoate?
cards.back_md: CH₃COONa + NaOH → CH₄ + Na₂CO₃ (soda lime, heat); one carbon fewer.

cards.front_md: Kolbe electrolysis: product at the anode?
cards.back_md: R–R (twice R), with CO₂; ethane from sodium ethanoate.

cards.front_md: Wurtz reaction?
cards.back_md: 2RX + 2Na (dry ether) → R–R + 2NaX.

cards.front_md: Why is the Wurtz reaction unsuitable for odd-carbon alkanes?
cards.back_md: Two different halides give a mixture of three alkanes that is hard to separate.

cards.front_md: Corey–House synthesis?
cards.back_md: R₂CuLi + R′X → R–R′ + RCu + LiX; clean synthesis of unsymmetrical alkanes.

cards.front_md: Reduction of an aldehyde to an alkane?
cards.back_md: Zn–Hg and conc. HCl: R–CHO to R–CH₃.

cards.front_md: Grignard reagent + water?
cards.back_md: RMgX + H₂O → R–H + Mg(OH)X.

cards.front_md: State and physical trends of alkanes?
cards.back_md: C₁–C₄ gases, C₅–C₁₇ liquids, then solids; density below 1 g mL⁻¹; insoluble in water.

cards.front_md: Why does the boiling point rise with chain length?
cards.back_md: Larger surface, stronger London dispersion forces.

cards.front_md: Effect of branching on boiling point?
cards.back_md: Lowers it: compact molecule, smaller surface, weaker forces.

cards.front_md: Boiling points of the three C₅H₁₂ isomers?
cards.back_md: Pentane 309 K, 2-methylbutane 301 K, 2,2-dimethylpropane 283 K.

cards.front_md: Combustion of an alkane CₙH₂ₙ₊₂?
cards.back_md: Gives n CO₂ and (n + 1) H₂O; needs (3n + 1)/2 O₂.

cards.front_md: Conditions for halogenation of alkanes?
cards.back_md: Halogen with ultraviolet or diffused sunlight, or 520–670 K.

cards.front_md: Three stages of the free-radical mechanism?
cards.back_md: Initiation, propagation, termination.

cards.front_md: Order of reactivity of C–H and of halogens?
cards.back_md: 3° > 2° > 1°; F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂.

cards.front_md: Catalytic oxidation of methane to methanol?
cards.back_md: 2CH₄ + O₂ → 2CH₃OH (Cu tube, 523 K, 100 atm).

cards.front_md: Aromatisation of hexane?
cards.back_md: C₆H₁₄ → C₆H₆ + 4H₂ (Cr₂O₃/Al₂O₃, 773 K, 10–20 atm).

cards.front_md: Isomerisation and pyrolysis?
cards.back_md: n-Butane → 2-methylpropane (AlCl₃/HCl, 573 K); large alkanes crack into smaller alkanes and alkenes.

questions.stem_md: A teacher hands out cards showing four hydrocarbons and asks which one is an alicyclic compound. The answer is:
questions.solution_md: Alicyclic compounds have a closed ring without aromatic character: cyclohexane, option (a). Benzene and methylbenzene are aromatic (b, d); hex-1-ene is an open-chain (aliphatic) alkene (c).

questions.stem_md: The carbon–carbon single bond in an ethane molecule is formed by the overlap of:

options.text_md: sp² hybrid orbitals, head-on, giving a sigma bond
unhybridised p orbitals, sideways, giving a pi bond
sp³ hybrid orbitals, head-on, giving a sigma bond
s and sp³ orbitals, head-on, giving a sigma bond

questions.solution_md: Each carbon of ethane is sp³ hybridised, so the C–C bond is a σ bond from head-on overlap of two sp³ orbitals — option (c). Options (a), (b) and (d) describe other hybridisations or a π bond.

questions.stem_md: An analyst at an oil refinery records the structure CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH(CH₂CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃ for a sample. Its IUPAC name is:
questions.solution_md: The longest chain has 7 carbons (heptane): CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–CH(C₂H₅)–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃. Numbering from the end nearer the first branch gives locants 2 and 4 (not 4 and 6). Alphabetically, ethyl comes before methyl: 4-ethyl-2-methylheptane, option (b). Option (a) breaks the alphabetical order, (c) the lowest-locant rule and (d) the longest-chain rule.

questions.stem_md: A student lists every chain isomer of heptane, C₇H₁₆, including heptane itself. The number of isomers is:
questions.solution_md: The numbers of chain isomers for C₄ to C₈ alkanes are 2, 3, 5, 9 and 18, so heptane (C₇) has 9 isomers — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The gas that bubbles up from decaying vegetation in a marsh, and is also the chief constituent of compressed natural gas, is:
questions.solution_md: Marsh gas, biogas and natural gas are mainly methane, option (d); ethane and propane are only minor constituents (a, b) and ethene is not a natural-gas component (c).

questions.stem_md: A Newman projection of ethane shows six C–H lines spaced at 60° intervals around the centre. This conformation is:

options.text_md: eclipsed, and the more stable of the two extreme forms
eclipsed, and the less stable of the two extreme forms
staggered, and the less stable of the two extreme forms
staggered, and the more stable of the two extreme forms

questions.solution_md: Six lines at equal 60° intervals mean that each rear bond lies midway between two front bonds: this is the staggered conformation, which has the least repulsion and the lowest energy — option (d). Options (a) and (b) call it eclipsed; (c) gets the stability wrong.

questions.stem_md: The torsional strain in ethane is greatest in the conformation in which:

options.text_md: each C–H bond on one carbon bisects the angle between two C–H bonds on the other carbon
the C–C bond is longer than 154 pm
each C–H bond on one carbon lies directly behind a C–H bond on the other carbon (dihedral angle 0°)
the molecule has a net dipole moment

questions.solution_md: Torsional strain arises from repulsion between bonding pairs on adjacent carbons. It is greatest when they are closest, with a dihedral angle of 0° — option (c). Option (a) describes the staggered form; (b) and (d) are not features of conformations.

questions.stem_md: Ethane is rotated about its C–C bond through one complete turn of 360°. The number of staggered conformations passed through, each a minimum on the energy curve, is:
questions.solution_md: Each methyl group has three C–H bonds, so the pattern repeats every 120°: minima (staggered) at 60°, 180° and 300°, and maxima (eclipsed) at 0°, 120° and 240° — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Sodium 3-methylbutanoate, (CH₃)₂CHCH₂COONa, is heated strongly with soda lime. The hydrocarbon formed is:
questions.solution_md: Decarboxylation replaces –COONa by –H: (CH₃)₂CHCH₂–H, which is 2-methylpropane — option (a). The product has one carbon fewer than the acid; (c) keeps the carboxyl carbon, while (b) and (d) have the wrong skeleton.

questions.stem_md: A concentrated aqueous solution of sodium butanoate is electrolysed between platinum electrodes. The organic product at the anode is:
questions.solution_md: In Kolbe electrolysis two R–COO⁻ ions give R–R. Here R = C₃H₇, so R–R is hexane — option (c). Propane (a) is what soda-lime decarboxylation would give; (b) and (d) join the wrong number of carbons.

questions.stem_md: A student wishes to make hexane in good yield by the Wurtz reaction, using a single alkyl halide and sodium in dry ether. The halide to choose is:
questions.solution_md: The Wurtz reaction joins two identical R groups, giving R–R with twice the carbons of R. Hexane has 6 carbons, so R = C₃H₇ and the halide is 1-bromopropane — option (b). The others give dodecane (a), butane (c) and octane (d).

questions.stem_md: Lithium dimethylcuprate, (CH₃)₂CuLi, is treated with 1-bromobutane in dry ether. The alkane formed is:
questions.solution_md: In the Corey–House synthesis R₂CuLi + R′X gives R–R′. Here R = CH₃ and R′ = C₄H₉, so the product is pentane — option (b). Hexane (a), butane (c) and ethane (d) would need other groups.

questions.stem_md: Propylmagnesium bromide, prepared in dry ether, is poured into water. The organic product is:
questions.solution_md: A Grignard reagent is hydrolysed by water to the alkane: C₃H₇MgBr + H₂O gives C₃H₈ (propane) and Mg(OH)Br — option (b). Propan-1-ol (a) would need oxygen insertion, hexane (c) is a coupling product and propene (d) needs elimination.

questions.stem_md: Butanal is warmed with zinc amalgam and concentrated hydrochloric acid. The main product is:
questions.solution_md: Clemmensen reduction converts the C=O group of an aldehyde into CH₂, so butanal, CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO, gives butane — option (b). Butan-1-ol (a) is only a partial reduction product; propane (c) has lost a carbon and but-1-ene (d) is unsaturated.

questions.stem_md: A sample labelled C₅H₁₂ boils at 301 K. Pentane boils at 309 K and 2,2-dimethylpropane at 283 K. The sample is most likely:
questions.solution_md: Branching lowers the boiling point: straight-chain pentane (309 K) > singly branched isomer > doubly branched 2,2-dimethylpropane (283 K). A value of 301 K lies between them, so the sample is 2-methylbutane — option (c). Options (a) and (b) are the isomers with the other two boiling points; cyclopentane (d) is C₅H₁₀.

questions.stem_md: Of the four isomers of C₆H₁₄ below, the one with the lowest boiling point is:
questions.solution_md: All four isomers have the same molar mass, so the one with the smallest surface area (most compact, most branched) has the weakest dispersion forces and the lowest boiling point: 2,2-dimethylbutane — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Liquid hexane is poured gently into a beaker of water and the mixture is stirred. After some time, the observation is:

options.text_md: two layers, with hexane at the bottom
a single layer that smells of an alcohol
two layers, with hexane floating on top

questions.solution_md: Hexane is non-polar and cannot form hydrogen bonds with water, so it does not dissolve; being less dense than water it forms the upper layer — option (d). It neither dissolves (a) nor sinks (b) nor reacts with water (c).

questions.stem_md: In the chlorination of methane in sunlight, which of these represents a chain-termination step?
questions.solution_md: A termination step removes two radicals by combining them into a molecule: •CH₃ + •CH₃ → C₂H₆ — option (d). Options (a) and (b) are propagation steps (a radical is regenerated) and (c) is initiation.

questions.stem_md: When 2-methylbutane is chlorinated in sunlight, the number of different monochloro structural isomers that can form is:
questions.solution_md: Count the hydrogen types in CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃: the two equivalent CH₃ groups on C-2, the C-2 H, the CH₂ hydrogens and the terminal CH₃. That makes 4 types of hydrogen, so 4 monochloro isomers — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Hexane is passed over a Cr₂O₃/Al₂O₃ catalyst at 773 K and 10–20 atm and is converted to benzene. The number of moles of hydrogen gas liberated per mole of hexane is:
questions.solution_md: C₆H₁₄ gives C₆H₆, so 14 − 6 = 8 hydrogen atoms are lost, that is 4 mol of H₂ — option (b). One mole (a) is lost in cyclisation alone and 3 mol (c) when cyclohexane goes to benzene; 7 (d) assumes all 14 H atoms leave.

questions.stem_md: Anhydrous aluminium chloride and hydrogen chloride at about 573 K convert n-butane mainly into:
questions.solution_md: These conditions bring about isomerisation of a straight-chain alkane to its branched isomer: n-butane gives 2-methylpropane — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A mixture of methane with a limited supply of oxygen is passed through a copper tube at 523 K and 100 atm. The main product is:
questions.solution_md: Controlled catalytic oxidation with copper under these conditions converts methane to methanol: 2CH₄ + O₂ gives 2CH₃OH — option (a). Methanal (b) needs Mo₂O₃; carbon dioxide (c) is the product of complete combustion; there is no chlorine present for (d).

questions.stem_md: Propane, C₃H₈, is burnt completely in a burner. The volume of oxygen at STP (molar volume 22.4 L) needed for 0.50 mol of propane is:
questions.solution_md: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O, so $n(\text{O}_2) = 5 \times 0.50 = 2.50\ \text{mol}$ and $V = 2.50 \times 22.4 = 56.0\ \text{L}$ — option (c). Option (a) is the volume of propane itself, (b) is the volume of CO₂ formed and (d) doubles the oxygen.

questions.stem_md: The fuel sold in a household LPG cylinder consists mainly of:
questions.solution_md: LPG is a mixture of butane and propane compressed to a liquid — option (a). Methane and ethane (b) are the main components of natural gas, and (c) and (d) are not used as LPG.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The staggered conformation of ethane has a lower energy than the eclipsed conformation.

**Reason (R):** In the staggered conformation the C–H bonding pairs on the two carbons are as far apart as possible, so the repulsion between them is least.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A: the minimum repulsion between bonding pairs lowers the energy of the staggered form — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** 2,2-Dimethylpropane boils at a lower temperature than pentane.

**Reason (R):** Both pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane burn completely in excess oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. The lower boiling point is due to the compact shape and smaller surface area of 2,2-dimethylpropane, not to its combustion products, so R does not explain A — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Methane reacts with chlorine in ultraviolet light to give chloromethane.

**Reason (R):** The reaction proceeds through ionic intermediates formed by heterolytic fission of the Cl–Cl bond.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: light causes homolytic fission, giving chlorine radicals, and the reaction is a free-radical chain — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The electrolysis of aqueous sodium ethanoate gives methane at the anode.

**Reason (R):** Hydrogen gas is liberated at the anode in this electrolysis.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are false: the anode product is ethane (with carbon dioxide), formed by coupling of two methyl groups, and hydrogen is liberated at the cathode — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Corey–House synthesis can be used to prepare an unsymmetrical alkane such as pentane.

**Reason (R):** Alkanes are insoluble in water.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. The insolubility of alkanes in water has no bearing on how an alkane is built from R₂CuLi and R′X, so R is not the explanation — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A mixture of bromoethane and 1-bromopropane treated with sodium in dry ether gives three different alkanes.

**Reason (R):** Each alkyl halide can react only with molecules of its own kind.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true: butane, pentane and hexane form. R is false: the radicals or organosodium compounds can couple with those from either halide, which is why a mixture is formed — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the eclipsed conformation of ethane the hydrogen atoms on the two carbons are as far apart as possible.
questions.solution_md: False. In the eclipsed conformation they are directly behind one another (dihedral angle 0°); it is the staggered conformation that keeps them farthest apart.

questions.stem_md: True or false? When one alkyl halide, RX, is treated with sodium in dry ether, the alkane R–R formed has twice as many carbon atoms as the group R.
questions.solution_md: True. Two R groups couple, so the alkane contains 2 × (carbons in R) carbon atoms.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Among isomeric alkanes, the more highly branched isomer usually has the higher boiling point.
questions.solution_md: False. Branching makes the molecule more compact and reduces the surface area, so the dispersion forces and the boiling point are lower.

questions.stem_md: In the Corey–House synthesis, lithium dialkylcuprate is made from an alkyllithium and copper(I) ___.
questions.solution_md: **Iodide**: 2RLi + CuI gives R₂CuLi + LiI.

questions.stem_md: The energy difference between the eclipsed and staggered forms of ethane, called the torsional barrier, is about ___ kJ mol⁻¹.
questions.solution_md: About **12.5** kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.stem_md: The reaction of an alkane with chlorine in sunlight proceeds by a ___ chain mechanism.
questions.solution_md: A **free-radical** chain mechanism: initiation, propagation and termination.

questions.stem_md: Match each reaction of alkanes in Column I with its reagent or conditions in Column II.
questions.solution_md: Halogenation needs Cl₂ with light; aromatisation uses the mixed oxide catalyst at 773 K; isomerisation uses AlCl₃ with HCl; the oxidation to methanol uses copper at 523 K and 100 atm.

questions.stem_md: Match each alkane in Column I with its approximate boiling point in Column II.
questions.solution_md: Boiling points rise with chain length: methane 112 K < ethane 185 K < propane 231 K < butane 273 K.

questions.stem_md: A sample contains 0.240 mol of ethane, all in the staggered conformation. Taking the torsional barrier as 12.5 kJ mol⁻¹, how much energy, in kJ, is needed to bring all the molecules to the eclipsed conformation?
questions.solution_md: $E = n \times \text{barrier} = 0.240 \times 12.5 = 3.00\ \text{kJ}$.

questions.stem_md: A sample of 1.44 g of an open-chain saturated hydrocarbon burns completely to give 4.40 g of carbon dioxide. How many carbon atoms does one molecule of the hydrocarbon contain? (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
questions.solution_md: $n(\text{C}) = \dfrac{4.40}{44} = 0.100\ \text{mol}$. For $\text{C}_x\text{H}_{2x+2}$ (molar mass $14x + 2$): $\dfrac{1.44}{14x+2} \times x = 0.100$, so $1.44x = 0.100(14x + 2)$, which gives $x = 5$. The hydrocarbon is C₅H₁₂ (M = 72; $1.44 \div 72 = 0.0200$ mol, which gives $5 \times 0.0200 = 0.100$ mol of CO₂).

questions.stem_md: A chemist heats 9.60 g of sodium propanoate with excess soda lime until the reaction is complete. What volume of ethane, in litres at STP, is obtained? (Na = 23, C = 12, H = 1, O = 16; molar volume 22.4 L)
questions.solution_md: CH₃CH₂COONa + NaOH → CH₃CH₃ + Na₂CO₃. $M = 96\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$, so $n = 9.60 \div 96 = 0.100\ \text{mol}$ and 1 mol gives 1 mol of ethane: $V = 0.100 \times 22.4 = 2.24\ \text{L}$.

questions.stem_md: Butane is monochlorinated in sunlight. A secondary hydrogen is 3.8 times as reactive as a primary hydrogen towards a chlorine radical (given). What percentage of the monochloro product is 2-chlorobutane?
questions.solution_md: Butane, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃, has 6 primary and 4 secondary hydrogens. Weights: $6 \times 1.0 = 6.0$ and $4 \times 3.8 = 15.2$. $\%\ \text{2-chlorobutane} = \dfrac{15.2}{6.0 + 15.2} \times 100 = 71.70 \approx 71.7\%$.

questions.stem_md: A student is asked to explain why the alkanes are called a homologous series. State what is meant by a homologous series, and give the general formula of the alkanes and the difference in mass between successive members.

answer.model_answer_md: A homologous series is a family of compounds with the same functional group (here only C–C and C–H single bonds), the same general formula, and successive members that differ by a –CH₂– unit, with a gradual change in properties. The general formula of alkanes is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, and successive members differ by 14 mass units.

questions.solution_md: Definition; formula; 14 u.

questions.stem_md: A hydrocarbon dealer is shown three samples, all of C₅H₁₂. Write the IUPAC names of the isomer with one methyl branch and the isomer with two methyl branches, and name the type of isomerism.

answer.model_answer_md: One methyl branch: 2-methylbutane. Two methyl branches (both on C-2): 2,2-dimethylpropane. The third isomer is straight-chain pentane. They differ in the carbon skeleton, so the isomerism is chain isomerism.

questions.solution_md: Two names; chain isomerism.

questions.stem_md: Ethane has a staggered and an eclipsed conformation, but methane has no separate conformations. Explain why.

answer.model_answer_md: Conformations arise from rotation about a C–C single bond, which changes the relative positions of the groups on the two carbons. Methane has no C–C bond, only four equivalent C–H bonds on one carbon, so there is only one arrangement; ethane has a C–C bond, so rotation gives different arrangements.

questions.solution_md: Need a C–C bond.

marking_scheme.step: Conformations come from rotation about a C–C bond
Methane has none, so a single arrangement

questions.stem_md: Describe how the eclipsed conformation of ethane appears in a Newman projection, giving the dihedral angle, and say why this form is less stable than the staggered form.

answer.model_answer_md: The three C–H bonds of the rear carbon, drawn from the edge of the circle, lie directly behind the three C–H bonds of the front carbon, which meet at the centre (drawn slightly turned so that they can be seen); the dihedral angle is 0°. The bonding pairs on the two carbons are closest, so repulsion (torsional strain) is greatest and the energy is higher by about 12.5 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.solution_md: Rear bonds behind front bonds; 0°; torsional strain.

marking_scheme.step: Rear C–H bonds directly behind front bonds, dihedral angle 0°
Closest bonding pairs: greatest torsional strain

questions.stem_md: Sodium pentanoate is heated with soda lime (NaOH and CaO). Write the balanced equation and name the alkane formed.

answer.model_answer_md: $\ce{CH3CH2CH2CH2COONa + NaOH ->[CaO][\Delta] CH3CH2CH2CH3 + Na2CO3}$. The alkane is butane, with one carbon less than the pentanoate.

questions.solution_md: Balanced equation; butane.

questions.stem_md: Show, with a balanced equation, how 2,3-dimethylbutane can be prepared by the Wurtz reaction from a single halide.

answer.model_answer_md: The halide is 2-bromopropane: $\ce{2(CH3)2CHBr + 2Na ->[dry ether] (CH3)2CHCH(CH3)2 + 2NaBr}$. Two isopropyl groups join to give 2,3-dimethylbutane.

questions.solution_md: 2-Bromopropane and sodium.

marking_scheme.step: Balanced equation with sodium and dry ether

questions.stem_md: Show by equations how propane may be prepared by the Corey–House synthesis starting from chloromethane and bromoethane.

answer.model_answer_md: Step 1: $\ce{CH3Cl + 2Li -> CH3Li + LiCl}$. Step 2: $\ce{2CH3Li + CuI -> (CH3)2CuLi + LiI}$. Step 3: $\ce{(CH3)2CuLi + CH3CH2Br -> CH3CH2CH3 + CH3Cu + LiBr}$.

questions.solution_md: Alkyllithium; dialkylcuprate; coupling with bromoethane.

marking_scheme.step: Coupling with bromoethane to give propane

questions.stem_md: Hexane is insoluble in water but dissolves readily in benzene. Explain, using the nature of the forces between the molecules.

answer.model_answer_md: Water molecules are held together by strong hydrogen bonds. Hexane is non-polar and cannot form hydrogen bonds or dipole interactions with water, so it does not mix. Benzene and hexane are both non-polar and are held by similar London (dispersion) forces, so they mix freely: like dissolves like.

questions.solution_md: Hydrogen bonding in water; like dissolves like.

questions.stem_md: A mixture of bromoethane and 1-bromopropane is warmed with sodium in dry ether. Name the three alkanes that can form, and explain why the Wurtz reaction is unsuitable for preparing an alkane with an odd number of carbon atoms such as pentane.

answer.model_answer_md: The alkanes are butane (from two ethyl groups), pentane (ethyl + propyl) and hexane (two propyl groups). A single alkyl halide gives only R–R, with an even number of carbons. To obtain pentane we must use two different halides, and then the two other symmetrical alkanes form as well, so the product is a mixture of three alkanes whose boiling points are close and which are hard to separate, and the yield of pentane is low.

questions.stem_md: Aqueous sodium propanoate is electrolysed between platinum electrodes. Write the half-reactions at the anode and at the cathode, name the alkane formed, and state which alkane would be formed if the same salt were heated with soda lime.

questions.stem_md: The boiling points of four isomers of C₆H₁₄ are hexane 68.7 °C, 2-methylpentane 60.3 °C, 2,3-dimethylbutane 58.0 °C and 2,2-dimethylbutane 49.7 °C. State how the boiling point changes with the number of branches, explain it, and say why the two isomers with two methyl branches differ.

answer.model_answer_md: The boiling point falls as branching increases: hexane (no branch) is highest, 2-methylpentane (one branch) is lower, and the two dimethylbutanes are lower still. Branching makes the molecule more compact, which reduces the surface area of contact between neighbouring molecules, so the London dispersion forces are weaker and less energy is needed to separate them. 2,2-Dimethylbutane, with both methyl groups on one carbon, is the more nearly spherical of the two and so has the lower boiling point (49.7 °C against 58.0 °C).

questions.solution_md: Falls with branching; smaller surface; 2,2- is more spherical.

marking_scheme.step: Compact shape, smaller surface, weaker dispersion forces
2,2-isomer more spherical, so lower than the 2,3-isomer

questions.stem_md: At 298 K, the quantity RT (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) is the typical thermal energy of a mole of molecules. Calculate RT in kJ mol⁻¹, compare it with the torsional barrier of ethane (12.5 kJ mol⁻¹), and use the comparison to explain why the staggered and eclipsed forms of ethane cannot be separated.

answer.model_answer_md: RT = 8.314 × 298 ÷ 1000 = 2.48 kJ mol⁻¹. The barrier of 12.5 kJ mol⁻¹ is only about 5.0 times RT, so collisions at room temperature easily supply the energy to cross it: the molecule rotates millions of times a second between staggered forms, passing through eclipsed forms, and no single conformation can be isolated. The staggered form is the more stable, so most molecules are found in it at any instant.

questions.solution_md: RT; comparison; free rotation.

marking_scheme.step: Barrier about 5 times RT: easily crossed
Conformations interconvert rapidly, so cannot be separated

questions.stem_md:
A computer model gives these relative energies for ethane (illustrative values, kJ mol⁻¹) at dihedral angles of 0°, 30°, 60°, 90° and 120°: 12.50, 6.25, 0.00, 6.25, 12.50.

(a) Which angles correspond to the staggered and which to the eclipsed conformation? Describe the Newman projection of each. [2]

(b) Calculate the energy needed to convert 2.00 mol of ethane from the most stable to the least stable conformation. [1]

(c) Explain why the staggered conformation is more stable and why the two forms cannot be separated at room temperature. [2]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) The energy is lowest (0) at 60° and highest (12.50) at 0° and 120°. So 60° is staggered (rear C–H bonds midway between the front bonds, six lines 60° apart) and 0° and 120° are eclipsed (rear bonds directly behind the front bonds). (b) E = 2.00 × (12.50 − 0.00) = 25.0 kJ. (c) In the staggered form the bonding pairs on the two carbons are farthest apart, so repulsion (torsional strain) is least; in the eclipsed form they are closest. The barrier is small compared with the thermal energy at room temperature, so the molecule rotates freely and the forms interconvert too fast to be separated.

questions.solution_md: Staggered 60°, eclipsed 0° and 120°; energy 25.0 kJ; torsional strain and low barrier.

marking_scheme.step: (c) less repulsion between bonding pairs in staggered form
(c) low barrier, free rotation, cannot be separated

questions.stem_md:
(a) Describe the mechanism of the monochlorination of methane in sunlight, giving the equation for each step under the headings initiation, propagation and termination. [3]

(b) Chloromethane is accompanied by dichloromethane, trichloromethane and tetrachloromethane. Why is this, and how can the yield of chloromethane be increased? [1]

(c) Arrange F₂, Cl₂, Br₂ and I₂ in decreasing order of their reactivity towards alkanes. [1]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Initiation: Cl₂ → 2Cl• (light). Propagation: CH₄ + Cl• → •CH₃ + HCl, then •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl• (repeated). Termination: any two radicals combine, e.g. Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂, •CH₃ + Cl• → CH₃Cl or •CH₃ + •CH₃ → C₂H₆. (b) Chloromethane still has hydrogen atoms, which a chlorine radical can replace in further chain steps. Using a large excess of methane makes chlorine radicals more likely to meet methane than chloromethane. (c) F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂.

questions.solution_md: Mechanism; further substitution and excess methane; halogen order.

marking_scheme.step: (b) further substitution and excess of methane

questions.stem_md:
(a) The boiling points of pentane, hexane, heptane and octane are 36.1 °C, 68.7 °C, 98.4 °C and 125.7 °C. Calculate the average rise in boiling point for each added –CH₂– group, in °C. [1]

(b) Explain why the boiling point increases as the chain gets longer. [2]

(c) Hexane, 2-methylpentane and 2,2-dimethylbutane boil at 68.7 °C, 60.3 °C and 49.7 °C. Explain the trend. [2]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Rise = (125.7 − 36.1) ÷ 3 = 29.87 ≈ 29.9 °C per –CH₂– group. (b) Alkane molecules are non-polar and held by London dispersion forces. A longer chain has more surface and more electrons, so the attraction between neighbouring molecules is stronger, and more energy is needed to separate them. (c) The three are isomers of C₆H₁₄. More branching makes the molecule more compact, which reduces the surface area of contact, so the dispersion forces are weaker and the boiling point is lower.

questions.solution_md: Average rise; dispersion forces; branching.

marking_scheme.step: (b) longer chain: larger surface, stronger forces
(c) smaller surface, weaker forces, lower boiling point

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write a balanced equation for the complete combustion of hexane, C₆H₁₄, using whole-number coefficients. [1]

(b) A sample of 4.30 g of hexane burns completely. Calculate the volume of oxygen consumed at STP and the mass of carbon dioxide produced. (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16; molar volume 22.4 L) [2]

(c) When hexane burns in a poor supply of air, carbon monoxide and soot may form. Write one equation for the formation of carbon monoxide and say why it is dangerous. [2]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) $\ce{2C6H14 + 19O2 -> 12CO2 + 14H2O}$. (b) $n(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{14}) = 4.30 \div 86 = 0.0500$ mol; $n(\text{O}_2) = 9.5 \times 0.0500 = 0.475$ mol, so $V = 0.475 \times 22.4 = 10.6$ L; $n(\text{CO}_2) = 6 \times 0.0500 = 0.300$ mol, so mass $= 0.300 \times 44 = 13.2$ g. (c) For example $\ce{2C6H14 + 13O2 -> 12CO + 14H2O}$. Carbon monoxide is a colourless, odourless gas that binds to haemoglobin in blood more strongly than oxygen does, so it prevents oxygen transport and is poisonous.

questions.solution_md: Equation; oxygen 10.6 L and CO₂ 13.2 g; carbon monoxide.
